With the last of the autumn light failing, a deep gloom had settled over the men of Fort Endurance, a gloom far deeper than the coming of the northern twilight. For three days they had watched the river for a sign of the supply canoe, and for three days the river had remained stubbornly, cruelly empty. The men sat huddled and morose, their work forgotten; for what use was reinforcing the stockade when their winter rations were likely at the bottom of the Grey Falls rapids? But, to sit and despair would not fill their bellies nor keep the frost at bay; something had to be done, a spirit had to be rekindled in them, lest the winter take them before the first snows even fell.

"There is no more to be gained by staring at the water, my friends," said Mr. Davies, the post's factor, his voice firm but not without kindness. "The men in that canoe were good men, the best on this river, and they knew the risks they ran. We will not dishonour their courage by giving ourselves up to misery! We have work to do, and by heaven we shall do it, for ourselves and for the memory of those who would have expected no less!" There was a stirring in the group at the factor's words: for as the good book says, "Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad." The men rose with a renewed, if grim, determination to set about their tasks; and, as soon as the last of the firewood had been stacked and the pelts in the storehouse secured against the damp, Mr. Davies himself taking a turn with the axe to show he was no idle master, the trappers grasped their tools with one hand while they cast a final, wistful glance downriver with the other, and went back to their duties. Some among them perhaps had the thought that, if the worst had indeed come to pass, their lost comrades were at least spared the hardship of the winter ahead!

CHAPTER ELEVEN. A FEARFUL RECKONING.

After the hard labour of the day, Mr. Davies did not feel much inclined for the quiet contemplation his study usually afforded him, though he went towards it as a matter of habit; and when he reached the door he found young Edward Finchley already standing there, but looking wan and distressed, as if some private grief gnawed at him. "What troubles you, Edward?" said Mr. Davies. "You seem more undone than the simple fear of a hungry winter would warrant?"

"Yes, I am, sir," replied the young man. "I cannot shake the feeling of dread concerning my younger brother, James, and why I did not protest more forcefully when he declared his intention to join this expedition; but then he was ever the adventurous one, and who would have thought a clerk's apprentice would be allowed such a perilous charge?"

"Fortune's wheel turns in odd ways," said Mr. Davies. "When was it you last had word from him in Montreal?"

"Six months ago come Martinmas, if my memory serves. He was then a green lad, not half so worldly as his letters pretended. How in creation did he convince the governor to let him travel? my mother had a mortal fear of the wilderness, and would never have given her blessing. But, there, it is my own fault for my prideful silence! As you once said, sir, I ought to have maintained my correspondence with my family, and then I should have known all of his plans. I cannot help but imagine all sorts of dreadful ends. My poor mother, who always held me in such high esteem, may be sick with worry; and my father, who has a weak heart, may--"

"Nonsense!" said Mr. Davies, clapping him on the shoulder. "If you continue in that vein, you'll imagine yourself a solitary ghost haunting these ramparts! Your brother James, as we must hope, will come strolling through that gate any day now and enlighten us as to how he came to be delayed; for we all know the river's fickle nature; and then you will learn all that you are now vexing yourself over, without any trouble. I confess I am curious in the matter too, for I wish to know the reason for the delay; but we must both hold to our patience, and put the subject from our minds for now. Come along with me, my boy," he added, as a shout went up from the men who had gathered by the water's edge. "I'm just going to see what this new commotion is about."

This sudden call to action at once caused the young clerk to start, just as the factor's earlier speech had aroused the men from their torpor. The news upon being heard proved even more startling than a canoe's appearance. "You see, Mr. Davies," cried Henri, the scout, gesticulating wildly towards the shore, "the river has turned out just as I feared it would, and my search up the bank proved fruitful. You are now, as I told you would be the case, in possession of the truth, or some part of it, though it is a grim prize!"

"You bet," chimed in a trapper named Silas, who seemed equally agitated and awed by the scout's discovery; but Mr. Davies could say little. The men's anxiety had until now prevented his truly believing the worst, and now that evidence was before him, all he could do was to silently stride towards the object Henri was pointing at; and after that each of the men who pressed near him did the same, full of a dreadful curiosity, and forgetting already their own fears for the future in the face of this tangible relic of the lost canoe. Their natural unease was perfectly redoubled a moment later, when Mr. Davies knelt and confirmed for all to see that the item half buried in the silt was a waterlogged travel chest, with the initials 'J. F.' clearly carved upon its lid.

The loud gasp with which the assembled men gave vent to their shock was so sharp that it seemed to cut through the evening air, and a young boy who was helping in the cookhouse dropped a pot with a clatter, as if seized by the same sudden terror. "It's James's," said Edward faintly; and at the same time his own legs, which had carried him to the spot, seemed to give way beneath him. "Where is he, Henri?" he said to the scout, his voice barely a whisper; "did you find anyone, Henri?"

"He is here with us," saith Henri, puzzled at the clerk's question; "but his chest arn't him, not by a long shot." The young man looked at the chest, and seemed to shrink. "No, it is not him. Oh, now I see it all!" and he covered his face with his hands and let out a single, dry sob, as if all the tears had already been spent inside him.

"There, there," said Silas, patting him awkwardly on the shoulder, "it's just a box, I tell you, lad; an' when Silas says so I guess he knows a box from a man!" But the clerk would not be comforted; and Mr. Davies, thinking that some harm might come to the lad's senses if he stood there staring, took him by the arm to lead him away. "Ahoy there, look sharp!" he shouted to the others, hardly knowing what he was saying, adding a moment afterwards, "Silas, you're needed! Get this to the storehouse."

"Here I am," cried Silas, moving to obey, with Henri after him. "What should we do with it, Mr. Davies?"

"I can't make sense of it now," said that worthy hopelessly. "He takes the sight of it to be a death warrant, an' when I try to speak he turns to stone and goes on quiet, that I'm afeard he'll fall down in a faint. Can't you say something, Edward; you were always a clever lad?"

"I'll try," said Edward, though his voice was choked; and turning back to the men, he drew a breath and spoke to Henri. "The lid! Look at the lid: is it broken?"

"Y-e-es," stammered he, "it--_it_ is splintered. But how did you know? It has been forced. Oh, my friends! where are you, and all the supplies?" And the scout burst out lamenting again, in a fit of despair which was painful to behold. Presently, however, he pried the lid open; and, in a stunned silence, Mr. Davies managed to get the truth from the chest's contents: a terrible truth of ambush, and piracy, and foul play on the lonely river. This was the story, as far as could be gathered from the disordered jumble within. James Finchley, much against his brother's better judgement, had packed not supplies in his personal chest, but a secret collection of valuable furs, which he had meant to trade for his own account at a distant, rival post.

"He must have taken it," he said, the words tasting like ash in his mouth. "He must have stolen it the night before they left. Oh, my brother, my brother! What have you done?" And the burly man looked up, in a state of confusion which was plain to see. Presently, however, he shook his head; and, with a new thought, Mr. Davies managed to piece together the likely story: a terrible story of greed, and mutiny, and a desperate fight on the lonely river. This was the narrative, as far as could be gathered from the evidence before them. James Finchley, in an act of utter desperation, had not only planned to betray the post with the furs, but had stolen the Company payroll, intending to disappear into the vast wilderness a rich man, leaving them all to their fate. But his own men, or perhaps some other party of river pirates attracted by the rumour of the payroll, had turned on him for the prize.

We will carry on our work, for to show fear is to invite attack; but, every man will have his rifle within arm's reach, whether he is in the mine or at the sluices. The afternoon's work was carried on with a kind of grim efficiency, the rhythmic scrape of shovels and the splash of water at the sluices punctuated by the sharp, metallic click of a rifle bolt being checked, or the quiet shifting of a weapon from one spot to a more convenient one. The sun began to dip towards the western peaks, painting the sky in glorious hues of orange and purple, but the men's eyes were fixed on the dark line of cottonwoods downstream, from which a thin curl of smoke now rose, a signal fire of trouble to come.

He motioned to Ernest, and together they walked towards the cabin, which now seemed less a simple dwelling and more a fortress, the last bastion of their hopes.

They found Frank, or Sailor Bill as the men still affectionately called him, much improved. The boy was sitting up in his cot, his face still pale but his eyes clear and intelligent; and, as they entered, he offered them a weak but genuine smile. Wolf, his faithful canine guardian, was lying at the foot of the bed, and thumped his tail in greeting but did not rise, his yellow eyes fixed on the door with watchful intensity.

"Much better, thank you, sir," Frank replied, his speech clearer now, though still bearing the cadence of one who has been through a great ordeal. "Seth has been a capital nurse, though he insists on calling me 'my b'y' and telling me stories about harpooning whales in the Arctic."

Frank's smile faded slightly, and a shadow passed over his face as his memory, now fully returned, brought back the terrible events that had led him here. "I remember everything now," he said in a low voice. "The ship... the 'Sea Serpent'... the storm. And the men... the mutineers." He shivered, despite the warmth of the cabin.
